newsitem.title: USA: Conservatives, arts backers slam U.S. House plan.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives, arts backers slam U.S. House plan.

text.p: Conservative pro-family groups and arts advocates Thursday slammed a plan by House Republicans to use federal block grants to fund arts programmes and wipe out the National Endowment for the Arts.

But the two groups were unhappy for very different reasons. Conservatives said the Republican measure would still give tax dollars to arts programmes that may yield works they find objectionable, while arts advocates said the plan would deprive small towns and rural areas of access to theatre, music and fine art now provided by the NEA.

"It is a failed and fooled strategy dreamed up by the Republican leadership, which is negotiating with itself," Patrick Trueman, governmental affairs director of the American Family Association, said.

The full House was to weigh in later in the day when it started considering a $13 billion spending bill mostly directed at federal lands programmes, which also included the NEA funding. The bill would slash next year's NEA funding to $10 million, enough to close down the agency, from about $100 million this year.

Democrats and some Northeastern Republicans pushed for a floor vote on an amendment to reinstate the $100 million but the House leadership blocked a vote. Instead they came up with a compromise plan to provide federal funds through $80 million in block grants to school districts and state arts councils.

"I think they are unwittingly destroying what I think is the greatest strength of the NEA, and that is to provide rural areas with access to culture," Judy Butler, executive director of Americans United to Save Arts and Humanities, said.

Butler said the new grants would be distributed according to population, meaning most would go to population centres that already have ready access to arts. She also said this was a last-minute scheme that is rife with questions.
"There's never even been a hearing on this," she said.

Several representatives of conservative and Christian groups said they expected the House to reject the compromise because it pleased neither conservative Republicans nor Democrats. Trueman said Republicans should have allowed the up-or-down vote on the NEA that Democrats sought even if the Democrats prevailed and kept the agency open for another year.
The Senate and White House will probably move to restore the NEA funding anyway, Trueman said. "At least we would get names and know who to go after," he added.
The block grant programme also carries the federal arts funding issue to the state level, making the fight to cut off the funding more difficult, he said.

"The new language still allows state arts councils to fund things that will be objectionable with federal dollars and that isn't the role of the federal government," Andrea Sheldon, executive director of the Traditional Values Coalition, said.

The National Assembly of State Arts Agencies also opposed the plan, which would send more money directly to them in the form of block grants. "The structure we have now has national leadership with grassroots results," Kimber Craine, spokesman for the organisation, said.
